oneIdea: Hard equations are solved by guess, improve, repeat. For one equation, bisection is safe but slow, Newton and secant are fast, and fixed-point depends on a good rearrangement. For many linear equations, Gaussian elimination turns the system into a triangle, and LU and Cholesky save that work so it can be reused.
goals: Rewrite \(f(x)=0\) as \(x=g(x)\) and run fixed-point iteration, using \(|g'(x^*)|<1\) to judge convergence.
Run bisection, Newton and secant by hand with a stopping rule \(E_n<\varepsilon\).
Choose a root-finding method by comparing what each needs (bracket, derivative, two guesses) and how fast it converges.
Solve a small linear system by forward elimination and back substitution.
Build \(A=LU\) and \(A=LL^T\) for small matrices and use them to solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) with two triangular solves.
Say when Cholesky applies (symmetric positive definite) and why pivoting matters.

intro.idea: A root of \(f\) is an input that makes the output zero: where the curve crosses the \(x\)-axis. Most equations cannot be solved by a formula, so we improve a guess step by step.
intro.mistake: Stopping when \(f(x)\) merely looks small, or after a fixed number of steps, without a clear tolerance. Always stop on \(|x_{k+1}-x_k|<\varepsilon\) (or a maximum iteration count).

check.q: Which value is a root of \(f(x)=x^2-x-2\)?
check.why: \(f(2)=4-2-2=0\). But \(f(1)=-2\) and \(f(3)=4\), so those are not roots.

fixed.idea: Rewrite \(f(x)=0\) as \(x=g(x)\), then keep feeding the answer back in: \(x_{k+1}=g(x_k)\). It settles on a value that \(g\) maps to itself, a fixed point.
fixed.mistake: Believing every rearrangement works. The same equation can be rewritten many ways, and only those with \(|g'(x^*)|<1\) near the root converge.

check.why: \(x_1=g(0)=1\), then \(x_2=g(1)=0.5+1=1.5\). The iterates (0, 1, 1.5, ...) are creeping towards the fixed point 2.

fixed-demo.idea: Each cobweb step is two moves: up to the curve (this computes \(g(x_k)\)), then across to the line \(y=x\) (this makes it the next input).
fixed-demo.mistake: Reading the picture as if the dots must always move towards the crossing. If the curve is steeper than the line \(y=x\) the cobweb spirals or steps away.

check.why: \(0.5\to0.25\to0.0625\to\cdots\to0\). Squaring a number below 1 shrinks it. Starting at \(x_0=2\) would give 4, 16, 256, ... instead.

fixed-example.idea: The table shows the error \(E_n=|x_{n+1}-x_n|\) shrinking by roughly the same factor every step. We stop at the first \(n\) where it drops below \(\varepsilon\).
fixed-example.mistake: Comparing the wrong quantity with \(\varepsilon\), for example checking \(x_n\) instead of the change \(E_n\), or rounding the numbers so hard that \(E_n\) looks like zero too early.

check.q: In the table, \(E_3=0.0002\) and \(E_4=0.00003\). With \(\varepsilon=10^{-4}\), when do we stop?

fixed-theory.idea: The error is multiplied by about \(g'(x^*)\) each step. Slope smaller than 1 in size: errors shrink. Larger than 1: errors grow.
fixed-theory.mistake: Treating the slope test as a global guarantee. \(|g'(x^*)|<1\) only promises convergence when you start close enough; the safe range of \(x_0\) needs the interval (contraction) condition.

check.q: Near the root \(|g'(x^*)|=0.5\) and the current error is 0.2. About what is the error two steps later?
check.why: Each step multiplies the error by 0.5: \(0.2\to0.1\to0.05\).

bisect.idea: If a continuous \(f\) is negative at one end of an interval and positive at the other, a root is trapped inside. Cut at the midpoint, keep the half that still changes sign, repeat.
bisect.mistake: Starting without a sign change. You need \(f(a)\,f(b)<0\); if both ends have the same sign the method may miss roots (two roots in the interval can cancel the sign change).

check.q: The width of the bracket after \(n\) cuts is \((b-a)/2^n\). Starting from \([0,8]\), how many cuts give a width \(\le1\)?
check.why: \(8/2^3=1\). After 2 cuts the width is still \(8/4=2\).

bisect-demo.idea: Watch the shaded bracket shrink by half each step; the root is never lost because the kept half always has a sign change.
bisect-demo.mistake: Keeping the half by guessing where the root 'looks closer'. The rule is only about signs: keep the half where \(f\) has opposite signs at the ends.

check.q: For \(f(x)=x^2-2\) on \([0,2]\), the midpoint is \(c=1\) and \(f(1)=-1\). Which half do we keep?
check.why: \(f(1)=-1<0\) and \(f(2)=2>0\): the sign change is in \([1,2]\). On \([0,1]\) both ends are negative.

bisect-example.idea: Every row halves the bracket, so the error bound \(E_n=\tfrac{b-a}{2}\) of the current interval halves too (0.5, 0.25, 0.125, ...).
bisect-example.mistake: Quoting the midpoint as exact. It is only guaranteed within \(E_n\), so report digits that the error bound supports.

check.q: The table starts with \(E_1=0.5\) and halves each step. What is \(E_5\)?

newton.idea: Replace the curve by its tangent line at the current guess and jump to where that line hits the axis: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\).
newton.mistake: Forgetting the minus sign or dividing the wrong way round (using \(f'/f\)). Also: starting where \(f'\) is near zero, which sends the next guess far away.

newton-demo.idea: A tangent leap lands very close to the root when you start nearby; the steps shrink dramatically.
newton-demo.mistake: Choosing a start where the tangent is nearly flat. A flat tangent hits the axis far away, so the iteration can jump to a different root or diverge.

check.q: For \(f(x)=x^2-2\), what goes wrong if you start Newton at \(x_0=0\)?
opts: \(f'(0)=0\), so the step divides by zero
check.why: \(x_1=0-(-2)/0\) is undefined. The tangent at 0 is horizontal and never meets the axis.

newton-example.idea: Newton's error is roughly squared each step (0.046, 0.00045, \(10^{-7}\)): the number of correct digits about doubles.
newton-example.mistake: Expecting the same fast speed from a bad start. Quadratic convergence only appears once you are close to the root.

check.q: A Newton iteration has error 0.001. About what is the next error?
check.why: Squaring: \((10^{-3})^2=10^{-6}\). Linear methods would only reduce it by a constant factor.

secant.idea: Same tangent idea as Newton, but the slope is estimated from the two latest points, so no derivative is needed.
secant.mistake: Using only one starting value. The formula uses \(x_k\) and \(x_{k-1}\), so you must supply two initial guesses.

secant-demo.idea: The orange line through the two latest points is the secant; where it crosses the axis is the next guess.
secant-demo.mistake: Mixing up the order of the two points in the slope. The slope \(\tfrac{f(x_k)-f(x_{k-1})}{x_k-x_{k-1}}\) is the same either way, but numerator and denominator must use the same order.

check.q: The latest two points are \((2,1)\) and \((4,5)\). What is the slope of the secant?

secant-example.idea: Look at the table: each row reuses the previous two values, and only one new \(f\) value is needed per step.
secant-example.mistake: Computing a new derivative at each step. The secant method never needs \(f'\).

check.q: Per iteration, what does the secant method need to evaluate newly?
check.why: The old \(f\) values are reused, so one new function evaluation per step (Newton needs \(f\) and \(f'\)).

compare.idea: Bisection is safe but slow, Newton is fast but needs \(f'\) and a good start, secant sits in between. Real solvers (like fzero) combine them.
compare.mistake: Picking the 'fastest' method blindly. Fast methods give no guarantee; if it must not fail, bracket first.

check.q: You have no formula for \(f'\), but want faster convergence than bisection. Which method fits?
check.why: Secant avoids derivatives and converges superlinearly (order about 1.62). Newton needs \(f'\).

gauss.idea: Use row operations to turn the system into a triangle, then solve from the bottom up. This is how you solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) by hand.
gauss.mistake: Dividing by a zero (or tiny) pivot. Swap in a row with a bigger pivot first (partial pivoting); MATLAB's \ does that for you.

lu.idea: Factor once into \(A=LU\), then every new right-hand side costs only two quick triangular solves. \(L\) stores the multipliers.
lu.mistake: Re-doing the whole elimination for each new \(\mathbf{b}\). Keep \(L\) and \(U\) and reuse them.

check.q: For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\6&5\end{bmatrix}\), what is the entry \(l_{21}\) of \(L\)?
check.why: \(l_{21}=6/2=3\) (the multiplier used to clear the 6). Then \(U=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\).

chol.idea: If \(A\) is symmetric and positive definite you can write \(A=LL^T\): half the work of LU, and a failed square root tells you the matrix is not positive definite.
chol.mistake: Applying Cholesky to a matrix that is not symmetric. Check \(a_{ij}=a_{ji}\) first.
